English

English Wikipedia has an article on:
ham
Wikipedia

Etymology 1

Inherited from Middle English hamme, from Old English hamm (“inner or hind part of the knee, ham”), from Proto-West Germanic *hammu, from Proto-Germanic *hamō, *hammō, *hanmō, from Proto-Indo-European *kónh₂m (“leg”).

Cognate with Dutch ham (“ham”), dialectal German Hamme (“hind part of the knee, ham”), dialectal Swedish ham (“the hind part of the knee”), Icelandic höm (“the ham or haunch of a horse”), Old Irish cnáim (“bone”), Ancient Greek κνήμη (knḗmē, “shinbone”). Compare gammon and gam.

    • (without /æ/ raising) IPA(key): [ˈhæːm]
    • (/æ/ raising) IPA(key): [ˈheːm] ~ [ˈhɛːm]
  • (New Zealand) IPA(key): /ˈhɛm/, [ˈhɛm]
  • Rhymes: -æm

Noun

ham (countable and uncountable, plural hams)

  2. (anatomy) The region back of the knee joint; the popliteal space; the hock.
  4. (countable) A thigh and/or buttock of a hog slaughtered for meat; (occasionally) the corresponding cut from some other animal.
    Hypernyms: cut; meat < food
    • 1931, Ion L. Idriess, Lasseter's Last Ride, Sydney: Angus and Robertson, page 165:
      "I'll have you so your hams will stand out like horse's shanks!" de declared.
  6. (uncountable) Meat from the thigh and/or buttock of a hog cured for food.
    Hypernyms: meat < food
    a little piece of ham for the cat
    • 2012, Audra Lilly Griffeth, A King's Daughter, →ISBN:
      She put some ham in the beans and cut up some sweet potatoes to boil.
  8. The back of the thigh of humans or certain other animals.
  9. (Internet, informal, uncommon) Electronic mail that is wanted; email that is not spam or junk mail.
    Synonym: ham e-mail
    Antonyms: spam, junk mail

Etymology 2

Inherited from Middle English ham, from Old English hām.

Noun

ham (uncountable)

  2. Obsolete form of home.
Usage notes
  • Persists in many old place names, such as Buckingham.
Related terms
  • hamlet

References

  • Douglas Harper (2001–2026), “ham”, in Online Etymology Dictionary.

Etymology 3

    Uncertain, though it is generally agreed upon that it first appeared in print around the 1880s. At least four theories persist:

    • It came naturally from the word amateur. Deemed likely by Hendrickson (1997), but then the question would be why it took so long to pop up. He rejects the folk etymology of Cockney slang hamateur because it originated in American English.[1]
    • From the play Hamlet, where the title character was often played poorly and/or in an exaggerated manner. Also deemed likely by Hendrickson, though he raises the issue that the term would have likely been around earlier if this were the case.
    • From the minstrel's practice of using ham fat to remove heavy black makeup used during performances.[2]
    • Shortened from hamfatter (“inferior actor”), said to derive from the 1863 minstrel show song The Ham-fat Man.[3] William and Mary Morris (1988) argue that it's not known whether the song inspired the term or the term inspired the song, but that they believe the latter is the case.

    Noun

    ham (plural hams)

    2. (acting) An overacting or amateurish performer; an actor with an especially showy or exaggerated style.
      Synonyms: hambone, hamfatter, overactor, tear-cat
      • 2023 June 13, Dwight Garner, quoting James Wood, “Cormac McCarthy, Novelist of a Darker America, Is Dead at 89”, in The New York Times‎, New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2 February 2026:
        Writing in The New Yorker in 2005, James Wood praised Mr. McCarthy as “a colossally gifted writer” and “one of the great hams of American prose, who delights in producing a histrionic rhetoric that brilliantly ventriloquizes the King James Bible, Shakespearean and Jacobean tragedy, Melville, Conrad, and Faulkner.”
    3. (radio) An amateur radio operator.
      Synonym: radio amateur
    Derived terms

    • hamfest
    • ham-fisted
    • ham radio
    • radio ham

    Chamorro

    Etymology

    From Pre-Chamorro *xami, from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *kami, from Proto-Austronesian *kami. Cognates include Indonesian kami and Tagalog kami.

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): /hæm/

    Pronoun

    ham

    1. we, us (exclusive)

    Usage notes

    • ham is used either as a subject of an intransitive verb or as an object of a transitive verb, while in is used as a subject of a transitive verb.
      I lahi ha sangani ham. ― The man told us.
    • In transitive clauses with an indefinite object, ham can be used as a subject.

    German

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): /ham/

    Verb

    ham

    1. (colloquial) contraction of haben; pronunciation spelling of haben
      Wir ham grad gefrühstückt. ― We've just had breakfast.
      • 2017 April 25, Martin Thoma, “Zeitlos hässlich”, in Die Tageszeitung: taz‎, Berlin: taz, die tageszeitung Verlagsgenossenschaft eG, →ISSN, archived from the original on 18 October 2026:
        Außerdem ist es ein bisschen obszön und spekuliert auf Empörung: Die kleinen Leute ham kein Geld und die Mode-Fuzzis geben 2.000 Euro für einen Ikea-Beutel aus!
        It's also a bit obscene and hopes to rely on outrage: Little people got no money, and the fashion types spend 2000 euros on an Ikea bag!

    Usage notes

    Usually used in the present or to form the perfect, though it may be seen in the infinitive as well. See also the pronunciation section at haben.

      North Frisian

      Pronoun

      ham

      1. (Föhr-Amrum, Mooring) Object case of hi: him, himself
      2. (Föhr-Amrum, Mooring) Object case of hat: it, (in practice chiefly) itself
      3. (Föhr-Amrum) Object case of hat: her, herself

      Alternative forms

      • (him): 'n (reduced form), höm (Sylt)
      • (it): at, et, 't (reduced forms), höm (Sylt)
      • (her): 't (reduced form), har (Mooring), höör (Sylt)

      See also

      Personal and possessive pronouns (Föhr-Amrum dialect)
      personal possessive
      subject case object case masculine referent feminine / neuter referent plural referent
      full reduced full reduced attributive independent
      singular 1st ik 'k mi man min minen
      2nd dü – di dan din dinen
      3rd m hi 'r ham 'n san sin sinen
      f or n hat at, 't at, 't
      plural 1st wi 'f üs üüs üüsen
      üsens
      2nd jam 'm jam jau jauen
      jamens
      3rd jo 's jo 's hör hören
      hörens
      • The reduced forms with an apostrophe are enclitic; they immediately follow verbs or conjunctions. Dü is deleted altogether in such contexts.
      • At is not enclitic; it can stand in any unstressed position and refers mostly to things. In reflexive use, only full object forms occur.
      • Dual forms wat / onk and jat / jonk are obsolete, as is feminine jü / hör.
      • Independent possessives are distinguished from attributive ones only with plural referents.
      • The forms üsens, jamens, hörens are used optionally (and decreasingly) when the possessor is a larger community, such as a village, city or nation.
      Personal and possessive pronouns (Mooring dialect)
      personal possessive
      subject case object case masculine

      full reduced full reduced

      The reduced forms with an apostrophe are enclitic; they immediately follow verbs or conjunctions. Dü is deleted altogether in such contexts.
      Et is not enclitic and can stand in any unstressed position; the full subject form hat is now rarely used. In reflexive use, only full object forms occur.
      Dual forms wat / unk and jat / junk are obsolete. Attributive and independent possessives are not distinguished in Mooring.

      Norwegian Bokmål

      Pronunciation

      • IPA(key): /ham/, [hamː]
      • Rhymes: -am
      • Hyphenation: ham

      Etymology 1

      Borrowed from Danish ham (“him”), from Old Danish hanum, the dative singular of han (“he”), subsequently generalized as an object form.[1] See han (“he”) for the pronoun's disputed earlier origin.

      Compare Old Norse hánum, honum, Swedish honom, Icelandic honum, Faroese honum and Norn honon (“him”).

      Pronoun

      ham (nominative han, possessive hans, plural dem)

      1. him; the object form of han (“he”), used as a direct or indirect object and after prepositions.
        Jeg så ham i går. ― I saw him yesterday.
        Hun ga ham en gave. ― She gave him a present.
        Vi ventet på ham. ― We waited for him.
        Synonym: han (“him”)
        • 1930, “Jobs bok”, in Bibelen‎, 9:13:
          Gud holder ikke sin vrede tilbake; under ham måtte Rahabs hjelpere bøie sig.
          God does not hold back his anger; beneath him the helpers of Rahab had to bow.
        • 1873, Henrik Ibsen, Kærlighedens komedie‎, page 25:
          hun blev ham og han blev hende tro
          She remained faithful to him, and he to her.
        • 1925, Herman Wildenvey, Fiken av Tistler‎, page 131:
          og gaar du paa gaten en dag med en herre, saa hviskes det ogsaa i klynger og klikker: Det er noget galt med ham der og han derre
          And if one day you walk down the street with a gentleman, people whisper in their little groups and cliques: There is something wrong with that fellow and that other one.
        • 1990, Jan Wiese, Kvinnen som kledte seg naken for sin elskede‎, page 10:
          bekreftelsen på Guds kjærlighet til oss og vår tro på Ham
          the confirmation of God’s love for us and our faith in Him
        • 1907, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Synnøve Solbakken”, in Bjørnstjerne Bjørnsons Fortællinger‎, page 98:
          Han far pryglte ham
          Father beat him.
        ham om det — that's his business; that's up to him.
        Hvis han vil nekte, så ham om det. ― If he wants to refuse, that's his business.
        • 2010, Lars Saabye Christensen, Bernhard Hvals forsnakkelser‎:
          ja, hva ellers, enn ham om det
          yes, what else but “that is his business”
        1. (metonymic) him; referring to a man's works, especially those of a writer or artist.
          Jeg liker Ibsen og leser ham ofte. ― I like Ibsen and often read his works.
          • 2016, Selma Lønning Aarø, Hennes løgnaktige ytre‎, page 167:
            Goebbels [skal] visstnok ha hatt ham på veggen hjemme
            Goebbels [is said to] have had him [i.e. pictures by Munch] hanging on the wall at home.
      2. (colloquial) Used before a male personal name when the name phrase is an object or follows a preposition.
        Jeg var hos ham Per i går. ― I visited Per yesterday.
        • 1909, Jacob B. Bull, Jutulskaret‎, page 100:
          efter al sorg med ham Kristen Storaker, som var faren
          after all the sorrow involving Kristen Storaker, who was the father
        • 1913, Ove Arthur Ansteinsson, Svartskogen‎, page 128:
          Det var det hun skulde hos ham Jens Svingen idag.
          That was what she was going to Jens Svingen’s to do today.
        • 1917, Hans Aanrud, Fortællinger for barn‎, volume I, page 159:
          Det har været værst for ham Kraakaaper
          It has been hardest on Kraakaaper.
        • 1923, Hans Aanrud, Jo-karerne i Skarvangen‎, page 160:
          du skal ta med dig Kristin til ham Storjo i Skarvangen
          You are to take Kristin with you to Storjo at Skarvangen.
      3. (dialectal) it; referring to the weather or conditions at sea.
        Vinden var sterk, men de trosset ham og rodde ut. ― The wind was strong, but they braved it and rowed out.
        • 1949, Andreas Markusson, Gjennom brenningen‎, page 14:
          de hadde seilt ham mange ganger før
          they had sailed in such weather many times before
      Usage notes
      • Ham and han are both standard object forms in Bokmål. The use of ham is optional; it does not require han to be avoided as an object.[2]
      • Ham is not an ordinary subject form. Both det er han and det er ham (“it is him”) are accepted as predicative constructions. Both forms also occur after comparisons: eldre enn han/ham (“older than him”).
      • The ordinary reflexive object form is seg (“himself”): Han så seg i speilet (“He saw himself in the mirror”), whereas Han så ham i speilet means “He saw him in the mirror”, referring to another person.
      • The pronoun is normally written with a lowercase initial, including when referring to God. Capitalized Ham occurs in religious writing.[3]
      See also

      • hans (“his”)
      • henne (“her”)
      • seg (“himself; herself; itself; themselves”)

      Etymology 2

      Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
      Ham (hudlag)
      Wikipedia no

      Inherited from Old Norse hamr (“skin; covering; shape”), from Proto-Germanic *hamaz (“covering; skin”), related to *hamô (“covering; skin”), of uncertain further origin. The guardian-spirit sense may reflect an older sense “caul”, associated in folk belief with a child's soul and protective spirit.

      Cognate with Danish ham (“skin; slough”), Icelandic hamur (“skin; form”), Swedish hamn (“shape; apparition”), Old English hama (“covering; skin”) and obsolete English hame.

      Noun

      ham m (definite singular hammen, indefinite plural hammer, definite plural hammene)

      1. (zoology) An animal's outer covering, especially one that is shed or renewed; skin, slough, coat or plumage.
        Slangen hadde lagt igjen hammen sin mellom steinene. ― The snake had left its shed skin between the stones.
        skifte ham, skyte ham, kaste hammen — to shed one's skin or moult.
        Slangen gjemte seg mens den skiftet ham. ― The snake hid while it was shedding its skin.
        • 1916, Ejlert Bjerke, Den sunkne lotus‎, page 152:
          mellem nogen sivstranter har en leviatan av en sandorm nylig skubbet sin hamm av sig
          Among some reed stalks, a leviathan of a sandworm has recently shed its skin.
        • 1932, Margarete Bonnevie, Ekteskap og arbeide‎, page 125:
          Hannene er utstyrt med de praktfulleste fjær og de vakreste hammer.
          The males are endowed with the most magnificent feathers and the most beautiful plumage.
      2. (figurative) A guise; an outward appearance, form or character.
        Den gamle restauranten åpnet igjen i ny ham. ― The old restaurant reopened in a new guise.
        • 1945, Solvejg Eriksen, Hele Norges Lalla‎, page 45:
          Chat Noir […] har den fjerde hammen på
          Chat Noir […] is wearing its fourth guise.
        • 1918, Gabriel Scott, Kilden‎, page 1:
          et menneske kommer til verden, det vandrer rundt i en ham av støv
          A human being comes into the world and wanders about in a guise of dust.
        • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, page 11:
          ja, en løgn kan endevendes, […] klædes i en nygjort ham
          Yes, a lie can be turned inside out […] and clothed in a newly made guise.
        skifte ham — to change one's appearance or character completely.
        Partiet har skiftet ham siden forrige valg. ― The party has transformed itself since the last election.
        • 1923, Bernhard Folkestad, Blaa hjul‎, page 45:
          markerne laa og skiftet ham
          The fields lay there changing their appearance.
        • 1918, Gabriel Scott, Kilden‎, page 107:
          da er de saa blide og snilde, […] at en kan tro de har skiftet ham
          Then they are so cheerful and kind […] that one might think they had become different people.
        • 2021, Jan Kjærstad, En tid for å leve, page 72:
          dette å kunne skifte ham, stige frem på en klippe og snakke som en annen
          Being able to change one’s guise, step forward onto a rock, and speak as someone else.
        skyte ham — to shed one form and assume another.
        Landskapet skyter ham når våren kommer. ― The landscape takes on a new appearance when spring arrives.
        • 2004, Levi Henriksen, Snø vil falle over snø som har falt‎, page 69:
          Se Glomma skyte ham fra å være svanger og flomdiger, til å bli slunken og full av sandbanker
          Watch the Glomma shed its skin, changing from swollen and heavy with floodwater to shrunken and full of sandbanks.
        kaste hammen — to cast off a guise or a restrictive outward form.
        På scenen kastet hun hammen og ble en annen. ― On stage she cast off her usual guise and became someone else.
        • 1945, Solvejg Eriksen, Hele Norges Lalla‎, page 205:
          Chat Noirs frispråk får folk til å kaste hammen av ufrihet og bundethet
          Chat Noir’s frank speech makes people cast off the guise of unfreedom and constraint.
      3. (folklore) A shape or form, especially an animal form, assumed through magic.
        Trollmannen viste seg i en ulvs ham. ― The sorcerer appeared in the form of a wolf.
        • 1879, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, Norske Folke- og Huldre-Eventyr‎, page 244:
          dette [mennesket] var hvidbjørnen, som kastede hammen af sig om natten
          This [person] was the polar bear, who cast off his animal skin at night.
      4. (folklore) An attendant or guardian spirit, sometimes heard or seen before the arrival of the person it accompanies; a vardøger.
        De hørte hammen hans i gangen før han kom hjem. ― They heard his forerunner spirit in the hallway before he came home.
        • 1844, Andreas Faye, Norske Folke-Sagn‎, 3rd edition, published 1948, pages 69–70:
          Paa nogle Steder kaldes de Følgie eller Fylgie, paa andre Vardøgl, Vardygr, Vardivil eller Valdøiel; og stundom Ham, Hugham og Hau.
          In some places they are called Følgie or Fylgie, in others Vardøgl, Vardygr, Vardivil or Valdøiel; and sometimes Ham, Hugham and Hau.
      5. (folklore) A ghost or apparition.
        De trodde den bleke skikkelsen var en ham. ― They thought the pale figure was a ghost.
        • 1911, Olaf Benneche, Rygnestadgutten‎, page 139:
          først tænkte de det var en ham; men saa forstod de […] det var et fattig menneske
          At first they thought it was a ghost, but then they realized […] that it was a poor human being.
        • 1909, Rikard Berge and Sophus Bugge, Norske eventyr og sagn‎, page 34:
          da [tussen] begyndte at blæse, blev det slig vind at gutten fór tilveirs som en ham og holdt paa at flagre op under taget
          When [the goblin] began to blow, such a wind arose that the boy flew into the air like a ghost and nearly fluttered up under the roof.

            Ōsrēd, þe wæs Norþanhymbra cining, æfter wræcsīþe hām cumenum ġelǣht wæs ⁊ ofslagen on XVIII Kƚ Octoƀ ⁊ his līc liġþ æt Tīnamūþe. ⁊ Æþelrēd cining feng tō nīwan wīfe, sēo wæs Ælflēd ġehāten, on III Kƚ Octobr̃. [WARNING: may be normalized]
            Osred, who was king of Northumbrian, was apprehended and slain on the 17th of October after coming home from his exile, and his body lies at Tynemouth. And King Aethelred took a new wife, whose name was Aelfled, on the third of October.
          • c. 989–992 CE, Ælfric of Eynsham, “The Assumption of St. John the Apostle” (IV), in Benjamin Thorpe, F.S.A., ed. and transl., The Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church, volume I, London: Richard and John E. Taylor, published 1844, page 60:
            Ða het se apostol ða bære settan, and cwæð, "Min Drihten, Hælend Crist! Arære ðe, Drusiana; aris, and ġecyrr hām, and gearca ús gereordunge on þinum hūse." Drusiana þa arás swilce of slæpe awreht, and, carfull be ðæs apostoles hæse, hām gewende. [WARNING: may be normalized]
            Then the apostle bade them set down the bier, and said, "My Lord, Jesus Christ! Raise thee, Drusiana; arise, and return home, and prepare refection for us in thy house." Drusiana then arose as if from sleep awakened, and, mindful of the apostle's command, returned home.
        2. property, estate, farm
